messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I have trained a PCount model and would like to use the result to make predictions for both abundance and detection rate against the same dataset that I trained the model on. But I had a few questions about best practices and interpreting the predictions:
What is the difference between the "fitted" function and the "predict" function? My understanding is that fitted just makes predictions against the training data, but I'm not sure that the results are exactly the same.
If I want to operate at the 0.05 significance level, and not all of the covariates in my model are significant at that level, then what impact would this have on the predicted values? It seems to me that the Predict function just applies all the covariates regardless of their p-value. Given the insignificant values have a small effect size, I don't think it would affect the predictions too much. Just wondering if there is a best practice around this.
Thank you!
Vatsal

I have been pouring over these inflated SE and Estimates for awhile now and I might have an idea, but I thought I would run in by the group.

y <- 1872 (104 days x 18 hours) (note first few hours on day one are all NAs but I need the NA hours due to dimension requirements)

Why can't unmarked handle my full data set?

Thank you!

Ashley

messages.body_plain:
It can be really hard to diagnose this error. Your description of the dataset is a bit unclear. Am I correct that the y-matrix is 29 x 1872?

It's possible that part of the problem is simply that unmarked cannot handle that many primary periods all at once with this model, particularly when there is a lot of missing data (which requires a bunch of additional math).

The design is a bit unusual relative to the way the model is most commonly used, where primary periods represent longer time periods such as seasons or years, and the colonization and extinction parameters make a bit more intuitive sense. In those cases we're typically dealing with at most 10-15 primary periods. That said there shouldn't be any specific mathematical reason why so many primary periods shouldn't work.

I would suggest even more experiments with subsets, i.e., iteratively increasing the number of included primary periods until you get the error, and look at what specifically changed around that point to see if you can identify anything unusual. I'm of course not familiar with your objectives/design, but I would perhaps also consider: do you really need to estimate "extinction" and "colonization" parameters here? Are you sure dynamic occupancy is the right framework?

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ashley,

You stated below your y matrix has 18 rows and 104 columns - is that right? If so this is not correct. You should have 29 rows (one per site/ARU; based on your original email). Then there should be a number of columns equal to the number of primary periods * the number of secondary periods per primary period (104 * 18 = 1872). The first 18 columns are primary period 1, the second 18 are primary period 2, and so on.

I'm not suggesting you actually use subsets of data for your final models, just that you use subsetting temporarily as a way to narrow down the specific configuration of data at which the model no longer works, which may help with further diagnosis of the error.

Here are some thoughts about your design more generally. Again I don't fully understand your objectives, so some of these things may not make sense. As with camera traps, ARUs present some challenges because they (for better or worse) allow you to manipulate your design to a degree after the fact.

1. I would reconsider whether you actually need to look at detection probability at the hourly scale. It sounds like you are trying to estimate how occupancy changes over a period of several months. Why not define several sub-periods within June-October, perhaps one per month. Each sub-period could be e.g. 5-7 days. Then these periods become your primary periods, and your secondary period is days. For each day, you determine if the species was detected at least once (1) or not (0). This may make the model significantly easier to fit.

2. Dynamic occupancy is best used when you are specifically interested in modeling colonization and extinction probability at sites, and how these parameters are affected by covariates. You can put covariates on *initial* (i.e., at time=1) occupancy, but you cannot directly estimate the effect of covariates on how occupancy changes over time. That seems like the question you actually want to answer here - how does the amount of a food source (which is changing temporaly) affect occupancy probability?

An alternative would be to take the design I described in (1) and reframe it as a 'stacked' model (search the listserv for more discussion). So instead of 29 sites each with, say, 5 primary periods (one per month), you would re-define sites to be unique combinations of site and period. That would mean 29*5 = 145 site-periods. Each of these would have a covariate value for food equal to the average food value for that site during that particular week/month. This would allow how to estimate how the amount of food is affecting occupancy probability, using a regular occupancy model.

Ken

So far I have resorted to using subsets of my data that correspond to whitebark pine and Clark's Nutcracker biological seasons (early, late summer and fall/post seed harvest). But  because it was a low cone year in my region I would like to model all of my data together, in an ideal statistical world.

Specifically, for this project I'm interested in whether gdistsamp() and distsampOpen() allow for random intercepts.

Thanks!
-Tom

messages.body_plain:
Hi group!

As part of my analysis, I’m exploring the use of N-mixture models, but I would really appreciate your advice on their suitability given the structure of my datasets, as in reality I only have 1 site to monitor. Here's a brief overview of the three monitoring methods I’m comparing:

Transect-based spotlight counts

One site divided into 4 transects

10 surveys per year (with double counts by citizen scientists—potentially treated as 20)

Monitored over 3 years

Nest occupancy surveys

295 sites (nests)

5 repeated surveys per year

Conducted over 2 years (occupancy by citizen scientists for 1 year only)

Thermal video surveys

One site - 1 long boat transect

15 survey nights per year, over 2 years

Video footage can be reviewed multiple times, allowing repeated counts of the same event

My key question is:
Are N-mixture models appropriate for this kind of structure, particularly when spatial replication is limited (as in the first and third methods)? Also, I’m curious whether repeated counts from different observers or from video replays can meaningfully improve detectability estimates under these models.

Additionally, if you’re aware of any courses, workshops, or labs where I could deepen my understanding of hierarchical models for ecological monitoring (especially N-mixture and occupancy models), I’d be very grateful for any recommendations.

Thank you very much for your time and consideration—I truly appreciate any guidance you can offer.

Best regards,
Julia Morais
PhD Candidate
Monash University

hi Julia,
 I would not recommend N mixture models for (1) simply because there are too few sites.   I think study (3) it would be potentially ok if you chop the transect into smaller spatial units.  Since the replicates are repeated views of the same video, you don't have to worry about the closure assumption and using sub-units of the transect make a lot of sense (so "yes" to your key question there).  Then you have sampling over time to worry about too which is a different matter. You might consider treating this temporal replicates as "units" too and then doing what we call "stacking the data" (look around for what that means...).

 We may be doing a workshop in Oregon this fall, so keep following the unmarked list for information.
regards
andy

hi Julia,
 Thank you for your kind words.
 Re: the use of transect halves as replicates.... this is a potentially good idea although it raises some modeling questions related to potential dependence among the units and the effect of that. I would be cautious about that in general but especially with a very small sample size, and 8 isn't too many anyhow!  Sample size requirements for these models are not too different from occupancy models and I generally tell people they might work well with 50 or more sites depending on the objective, complexity of the model and so forth.  There are a lot of simulation studies published (see the original paper from 2004 and also the AHM1 book by Marc Kery and myself).  I just don't think you have enough data in that case study ...  But you should explore the model as a way of learning about its performance and limitations -- simulation is a great exercise to learn about a model and also to learn about your system.

 Re: the workshop, -- we're just in the very early stages of planning right now but, to be honest, I doubt highly that we would have an online platform. We don't have a lot of support to do these workshops and that requires technical support at a significant level and, in addition, it would diminish the in-person vibe and also a lot of people would choose that option instead of in-person, which further diminishes the workshop atmosphere.

regards
andy

Thank you so much for getting back to me again!

Apologies for circling back, but I had one more (possibly naïve) question about replication. You mentioned that for the video method, temporal replicates could potentially be treated as sampling units—essentially stacking them as "sites" within a year. Would something similar be valid for the small dataset from the spotlighting method too?

In that case, citizen scientists conducted repeat counts at the same 8 chopped sites, about 20 minutes after the expert survey, and from a different direction. This was repeated across three years. The transects are continuous, and the species is penguins—so they’re mobile, but not dramatically so, and although they respond mildly to observers, we include a 20-minute pause between surveys/observers to let them settle back into baseline behavior.

I was wondering if it would be reasonable to treat those second surveys as additional spatial units—i.e., stack them in the same way, making it 8 sites × 2 observer directions × 3 years = 48 spatial units. Would that be conceptually okay as a way to explore the model, or do you think the dependence and movement between adjacent units (especially in continuous space) would invalidate that approach? My goal at this point isn’t necessarily to produce robust ecological inference for management action, but rather to learn how the model behaves with data that stretch or challenge assumptions a bit—and also to compare different sampling methods for this unusual urban colony.

As for the workshop—totally understand, and I really appreciate the importance of the in-person format. I’ll do my best to attend! Though I have to say, suggesting an online version felt a bit like modeling: maybe not perfect, but sometimes it’s valid to try and see what happens! In the meantime, I’ll be trimming the video files and getting everything prepped.

Thanks again for your patience and generosity in answering these questions. I'm just trying to learn and understand the tools better, and your insight really helps.

Best regards,
Julia

my colleague Joanie Van de Walle just asked whether it was possible for me to post two advertised positions in her lab. My answer was: yes, I am very happy to do this. However, I'd like to note that anybody can post such adverts directly, provided that topically they fall within the scope of one of these lists. They use Bayesian IPMs to model population dynamics, quantify the mechanistic linkages between environmental factors and demographic rates, and project future population trajectories under scenarios of climate change and future exploitation levels.

Best regards  --- Marc

hi Julia,
 Yes I think you can use a "time for space" substitution (temporal replicates as sample units) in general but it's important to think carefully about the interpretation and also you must still have true replicate samples of each 'unit'. I'm not sure I would feel comfortable recommending it for your spotlighting survey, there seems to be a lot going on there, but it might work out depending on what your questions are. I guess from the standpoint of exploring the limitations of the method and understanding efficacy, you might as well try it out and see how things work out.

 Good luck!
regards
andy

I have decided to go with a pcountOpen/N mixture DM model in an attempt to use all of data at once and quantify time spent/abundance in burned areas by nutcrackers. This model is proving to be very slow.... I want to know if this is the best way forward? I have been reading the AHM2 book and they do mention the model time constraints.. I am worried because I don't have a firm grasp on the statistics, so if I am doing something incorrectly it will just cost me time. I have a complex model and when I run the residuals, they don't fit the data well. I am struggling to diagnose the model since unmarked data frames don't allow the use of the Dharma package... I am trying to determine how much time clark's nutcrackers are spending at each site per day (they may be caching seeds at these sites) so I am not interested in per hour differences, but am interested in daily time spent overall. I don't want to reduce presence/absence to per day because I would loose the fine scale hourly timing. With that I am using covariates, such as whitebark pine density, etc to measure occupancy probability.
>
> I originally was thinking of using 14 weeks as primary periods and 7 days as my secondary, but that seems too broad to get at my question. Maybe not? And yes your second point is what I would like to do, AND (most importantly) also determine if they are using certain sites that have been disturbed by fire. So there are static covariates and temporal covariates. Which complicates things.
>
> So far I have resorted to using subsets of my data that correspond to whitebark pine and Clark's Nutcracker biological seasons (early, late summer and fall/post seed harvest). But  because it was a low cone year in my region I would like to model all of my data together, in an ideal statistical world.

> > Hi Ashley,

> > You stated below your y matrix has 18 rows and 104 columns - is that right? If so this is not correct. You should have 29 rows (one per site/ARU; based on your original email). Then there should be a number of columns equal to the number of primary periods * the number of secondary periods per primary period (104 * 18 = 1872). The first 18 columns are primary period 1, the second 18 are primary period 2, and so on.
> >
> > I'm not suggesting you actually use subsets of data for your final models, just that you use subsetting temporarily as a way to narrow down the specific configuration of data at which the model no longer works, which may help with further diagnosis of the error.
> >
> > Here are some thoughts about your design more generally. Again I don't fully understand your objectives, so some of these things may not make sense. As with camera traps, ARUs present some challenges because they (for better or worse) allow you to manipulate your design to a degree after the fact.
> >
> > 1. I would reconsider whether you actually need to look at detection probability at the hourly scale. It sounds like you are trying to estimate how occupancy changes over a period of several months. Why not define several sub-periods within June-October, perhaps one per month. Each sub-period could be e.g. 5-7 days. Then these periods become your primary periods, and your secondary period is days. For each day, you determine if the species was detected at least once (1) or not (0). This may make the model significantly easier to fit.
> >
> > 2. Dynamic occupancy is best used when you are specifically interested in modeling colonization and extinction probability at sites, and how these parameters are affected by covariates. You can put covariates on *initial* (i.e., at time=1) occupancy, but you cannot directly estimate the effect of covariates on how occupancy changes over time. That seems like the question you actually want to answer here - how does the amount of a food source (which is changing temporaly) affect occupancy probability?
> >
> > An alternative would be to take the design I described in (1) and reframe it as a 'stacked' model (search the listserv for more discussion). So instead of 29 sites each with, say, 5 primary periods (one per month), you would re-define sites to be unique combinations of site and period. That would mean 29*5 = 145 site-periods. Each of these would have a covariate value for food equal to the average food value for that site during that particular week/month. This would allow how to estimate how the amount of food is affecting occupancy probability, using a regular occupancy model.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Anam,

for multispecies Nmix model, you'd normally use one of the Bayesian engines, JAGS, NIMBLE or even Stan. However, it should be possible to fit this model with function pcount() in unmarked, by stacking data for all species and adopting species-level random effects.

Best regards  --- Marc

> On Fri, Apr 25, 2025 at 12:08 PM 'Julia Braga Morais' via unmarked <unma...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Andy,
> >
> > Thank you so much for getting back to me again!
> >
> > Apologies for circling back, but I had one more (possibly naïve) question about replication. You mentioned that for the video method, temporal replicates could potentially be treated as sampling units—essentially stacking them as "sites" within a year. Would something similar be valid for the small dataset from the spotlighting method too?
> >
> > In that case, citizen scientists conducted repeat counts at the same 8 chopped sites, about 20 minutes after the expert survey, and from a different direction. This was repeated across three years. The transects are continuous, and the species is penguins—so they’re mobile, but not dramatically so, and although they respond mildly to observers, we include a 20-minute pause between surveys/observers to let them settle back into baseline behavior.
> >
> > I was wondering if it would be reasonable to treat those second surveys as additional spatial units—i.e., stack them in the same way, making it 8 sites × 2 observer directions × 3 years = 48 spatial units. Would that be conceptually okay as a way to explore the model, or do you think the dependence and movement between adjacent units (especially in continuous space) would invalidate that approach? My goal at this point isn’t necessarily to produce robust ecological inference for management action, but rather to learn how the model behaves with data that stretch or challenge assumptions a bit—and also to compare different sampling methods for this unusual urban colony.
> >
> > As for the workshop—totally understand, and I really appreciate the importance of the in-person format. I’ll do my best to attend! Though I have to say, suggesting an online version felt a bit like modeling: maybe not perfect, but sometimes it’s valid to try and see what happens! In the meantime, I’ll be trimming the video files and getting everything prepped.
> >
> > Thanks again for your patience and generosity in answering these questions. I'm just trying to learn and understand the tools better, and your insight really helps.
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Julia
> >
> > On Fri, 25 Apr 2025 at 09:58, Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > hi Julia,
> > >  Thank you for your kind words.
> > >  Re: the use of transect halves as replicates.... this is a potentially good idea although it raises some modeling questions related to potential dependence among the units and the effect of that. I would be cautious about that in general but especially with a very small sample size, and 8 isn't too many anyhow!  Sample size requirements for these models are not too different from occupancy models and I generally tell people they might work well with 50 or more sites depending on the objective, complexity of the model and so forth.  There are a lot of simulation studies published (see the original paper from 2004 and also the AHM1 book by Marc Kery and myself).  I just don't think you have enough data in that case study ...  But you should explore the model as a way of learning about its performance and limitations -- simulation is a great exercise to learn about a model and also to learn about your system.
> > >
> > >  Re: the workshop, -- we're just in the very early stages of planning right now but, to be honest, I doubt highly that we would have an online platform. We don't have a lot of support to do these workshops and that requires technical support at a significant level and, in addition, it would diminish the in-person vibe and also a lot of people would choose that option instead of in-person, which further diminishes the workshop atmosphere.
> > >
> > > regards
> > > andy

> > > >
> > > > Regarding Method 1, I actually have a bit more structure than I initially described. Each transect was surveyed in pairs, with counts recorded separately from the left and right sides. I had been summing these for simplicity, partly because we were tracking a biological observational covariate (the proportion of birds in a particular behavioural state), which was calculated per transect rather than per side. But now, thinking in terms of spatial replication, I realize I could potentially treat these as 8 separate sites instead of 4. Do you think that would improve the model's suitability in this case?
> > > >
> > > > I’ll also explore “stacking the data” as you suggested—it seems like a very promising approach to deal with the temporal aspect, as perhaps doing a time-for- space substitution would require more years of surveys.
> > > > Lastly, I’d be very keen to attend the Oregon workshop if there’s any possibility of joining virtually. I’ll definitely keep an eye on the unmarked list for updates.

Then you have sampling over time to worry about too which is a different matter. You might consider treating this temporal replicates as "units" too and then doing what we call "stacking the data" (look around for what that means...).

> > > > > > As part of my analysis, I’m exploring the use of N-mixture models, but I would really appreciate your advice on their suitability given the structure of my datasets, as in reality I only have 1 site to monitor. Here's a brief overview of the three monitoring methods I’m comparing:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Transect-based spotlight counts
> > > > > >
> > > > > > One site divided into 4 transects
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 10 surveys per year (with double counts by citizen scientists—potentially treated as 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Monitored over 3 years
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Nest occupancy surveys
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 295 sites (nests)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 5 repeated surveys per year
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Conducted over 2 years (occupancy by citizen scientists for 1 year only)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thermal video surveys
> > > > > >
> > > > > > One site - 1 long boat transect
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 15 survey nights per year, over 2 years
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Video footage can be reviewed multiple times, allowing repeated counts of the same event
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My key question is:
> > > > > > Are N-mixture models appropriate for this kind of structure, particularly when spatial replication is limited (as in the first and third methods)? > > > > > >
> > > > > > Additionally, if you’re aware of any courses, workshops, or labs where I could deepen my understanding of hierarchical models for ecological monitoring (especially N-mixture and occupancy models), I’d be very grateful for any recommendations.

> > > > > > Thank you very much for your time and consideration—I truly appreciate any guidance you can offer.
